- the elements of $S$ can be paired with the elements of $T$ so that the elements in each pair differ by exactly $1$.

The problem asks for the least number of elements the set $S$ can have such that $S$ has exactly 4040 cousins. Two sets $S$ and $T$ are cousins if they have the same size, are disjoint, and there exists a perfect matching between them consisting of edges in the integer graph (i.e., $|x-y|=1$). This is equivalent to partitioning $S \cup T$ into disjoint pairs of adjacent integers $\{x, x+1\}$ such that $S$ contains exactly one element from each pair and $T$ contains the other.

Let $k = |S| = |T|$. The set $S$ must be a subset of vertices in the integer graph. A valid matching covers every element in $S$ with a neighbor. Since $S$ and $T$ are disjoint, this is a matching of size $k$ in the graph.
Let $N(S)$ be the number of such neighbors sets $T$.
The maximum number of cousins for a set $S$ of size $k$ is $2^k$, which is achieved when the gaps between elements of $S$ are all at least 3. This is because if the distance between any two elements $u, v \in S$ is large enough, the edges connected to them are disjoint, allowing any of the 2 choices (left or right neighbor) for each element.
